# 1 Clement Chapter 33 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 1 Clement 33 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/1CL_033_page_001.jpg

---

## Chapter 33

**33:1** What then shall we do, brothers? Shall we grow idle from good works and abandon love? May the Master never permit this to happen to us; but let us press forward with earnestness and zeal to accomplish every good work.

**33:2** For the Creator and Master of all things himself rejoices in his own works.

**33:3** For by his all-powerful majesty he established the heavens, and by his incomprehensible understanding he set them in order; and the earth he separated from the water surrounding it and fixed it upon the sure foundation of his own will; and by his command he called into being the living creatures that walk upon it; and having prepared beforehand the sea and the living creatures in it, he enclosed them by his power.

**33:4** Above all, as the most excellent and by far the greatest work of his understanding, with his holy and faultless hands he formed man in the likeness of his own image.

**33:5** For God said: "Let us make man according to our image and our likeness. And God made man; male and female he made them."

**33:6** Having completed all these things, he praised and blessed them and said: "Be fruitful and multiply."

**33:7** Let us observe that all the righteous were adorned with good works; and even the Lord himself, adorning himself with works, rejoiced.

**33:8** Having therefore this pattern before us, let us without delay give ourselves to his will, and with all our strength let us perform the works of righteousness.

---

## Translator's Note

Chapter 33 provides the theological foundation for the call to good works after the justification-by-faith statement of ch. 32. The argument is: justification is by faith, not works — but this does not mean inactivity. Why? Because God himself delights in his works and formed humanity in his image (vv. 2-6). Therefore, doing good works is *imitating God*, not earning salvation. The creation narrative (vv. 3-6) is Clement's own retelling, blending Genesis 1 with a Stoic cosmological framework. The divine image statement in v. 4 places humanity as the "crown" of creation. "Be fruitful and multiply" (v. 6) is Genesis 1:28.

---

*SOPHIA represents the consensus translation, balancing literalness and clarity.*
